findings.summary: Page 1 describes the goroutine free list as "per-P" two pages before `P` is defined.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "Dead `g`s go on a per-P free list (`gFree`) and recycle." and the callout "Spawn-and-die churn reuses `g` structs off `gFree`". `P` is first defined on page 3: ["`P`","processor","permit + queue"].
findings.fix: On page 1 say "dead `g`s go on a runtime free list (`gFree`) and are recycled" and add the "per-P" qualifier on page 3 or 4, once P and its per-P resources are on the table.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: The claim that Java virtual threads pin on `synchronized` has been false since JDK 24 (JEP 491, March 2025), which made monitors virtual-thread-aware.
findings.fix: Change the cell to something like "pinned on `synchronized` pre-JDK 24; now only pins in native/JNI frames" (JEP 491 "Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning", delivered in JDK 24).

findings.summary: The cross-runtime comparison table (syllabus chapter 10 material) is placed on page 2, before the scheduler model, stacks and channels that make its rows meaningful.
findings.evidence: Page 2 table rows: ["Java virtual thread","pins on `synchronized`"], ["Erlang process","isolated heaps + supervision"], ["Thread pool","no queue-head blocking"] — appearing before page 3 introduces G/M/P and page 7 introduces growing stacks. The syllabus places all of these in the final chapter, "Trade-offs, Comparisons, and Summary".
findings.fix: Cut the "Against Other Runtimes" table from page 2 (leaving the loop-variable material, which does belong in chapter 1) and restore it to the closing comparison section, where P handoff, stack growth and backpressure have already been taught.

findings.summary: The "Run Queues" ring diagram has overlapping cells whose labels are clipped, so the first and last slots are unreadable.
findings.evidence: Leftmost cell reads "runne" with the rest cut off by the cell border, and the final cell's "global" text runs past its box and collides with the adjacent arrow box containing "→"; the columns are indexed 0–6 but only 6 visible cells line up under them.
findings.fix: Widen the diagram cells (or shrink the label font) so "runnext" and "global" fit inside their boxes, and give the trailing arrow box its own column instead of overlapping the last cell.

findings.summary: Page 4 explains the syscall handoff using `sysmon`, `retake` and `_Psyscall`, none of which are defined until page 6.
findings.evidence: Page 4: "M enters a syscall → its P goes to `_Psyscall`, still attached." / "Long syscall (or queued work): `sysmon`/`entersyscallblock` calls `handoffp`, another M picks it up." / "A core is idled only for the retake delay." Page 6 then introduces the term for the first time under the heading "sysmon, the Watcher": "A monitor thread that runs without a P." and "Runs long: `sysmon` calls `retake`, hands the P to another M."
findings.fix: On page 4 keep only the one-line handoff statement from the syllabus ("if an M blocks in a syscall, its P is detached and handed to another M so the other goroutines keep running") and move the `_Psyscall`/`entersyscallblock`/`handoffp`/retake-delay detail into page 6's "The Syscall Path" section, where `sysmon` is already defined.

findings.summary: Page 5 ends with a block critiquing cooperative and async preemption before either mechanism has been introduced (page 6 defines both), and that block also wedges itself between the `schedtrace` command and the table that explains its output.
findings.evidence: Page 5 final bullets: "Cooperative gap: tight loop, no calls, no allocation = never yields." / "Async preemption needed a compiler change, not just a runtime one." — while page 6 is where preemption is first defined: cards titled "Cooperative (all)" and "Async (1.14+)". The same block sits directly after page 5's `GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000 ./app` code, while the table that reads that output (`runqueue=`, `[2 0 5 1]`, `idleprocs`, `spinningthreads`) opens page 6.
findings.fix: Move the four cooperative/async-preemption bullets to page 6, immediately after the "Two Preemptions" cards; that also puts the schedtrace field table adjacent to the `GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000` code block it explains.

findings.summary: The "A Channel Is hchan" field diagram has truncated cell labels and an overlapping box.
findings.evidence: Cells read "ring | elem | coun | lock | send | recvq" — "coun" is cut short of "count" and "sendq"/"recvq" are clipped at the box edges, while the "buf" box sits on top of the "ring" cell above it.
findings.fix: Size the hchan cells to the widest field name (or abbreviate consistently, e.g. buf/elem/count/lock/sendq/recvq) and move the "buf" label out of the cell row so it no longer overlaps.

findings.summary: Page 8 closes with a `select` code example whose entire point is the nil-channel-disables-a-case trick, which is not explained until page 9.
findings.evidence: Page 8 code: "case <-done: in = nil  // disable case". Page 9 is where the rule appears — panic table row ["op on nil chan","blocks forever"] and the callout "nil is a feature": "set a `select` case's channel to nil to switch that case off for good."
findings.fix: Move that code block to page 9, directly under the "nil is a feature" callout, and let page 8 end with the `hchan` heading and diagram as the bridge into the channel page.

findings.summary: Page 10 opens with explanation blocks whose code and headings are stranded on page 9, so the semaphore bullets read as a continuation of the worker pool.
findings.evidence: Page 9 ends with heading "Semaphore" plus `sem := make(chan struct{}, N)` and no explanation; page 10's fifth block is an unheaded bullet list "A buffered channel of size N is the whole implementation. … Different goal than a pool: one goroutine per item still." placed immediately after the Worker Pool bullets. The same split affects `wg.Add(1)` (page 9 code) and the sidebox "Add-before-go" that explains it (page 10, first block).
findings.fix: Keep each pattern's heading, code and bullets on the same page: move the "Semaphore" heading and code to page 10 directly above its bullets (after the worker pool), and move the "Add-before-go" sidebox back to page 9 next to the `wg.Add(1)` code.

findings.summary: Page 1's closing callout uses "colouring" as a known concept, but the term is never defined in this content.
findings.evidence: Page 1 callout "Cheap, not free": "No colouring, no pool-size tuning — but also **no** built-in backpressure." The only other occurrence is a bare page 2 table cell, ["async/await","no function colouring"], which also does not define it.
findings.fix: Either drop "no colouring" from the page 1 callout, or define it in one clause where it is first used ("no function colouring — a blocking call does not force every caller to become async").

findings.summary: The snippet illustrates pre-1.22 loop-variable capture using `for i := range 3`, a range-over-int form that does not compile before Go 1.22, so it could never have "printed 3,3,3".
findings.evidence: ["for i := range 3 {","    go func(){ fmt.Println(i) }()  // 1.22+: safe","}  // pre-1.22 printed 3,3,3"]
findings.fix: Use a form valid in both eras for the historical comparison, e.g. `for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {` (and keep the `range 3` form only where it is labelled 1.22+).

findings.summary: `GODEBUG=scheddetail=1` alone prints nothing — the detailed per-G/M/P dump requires `schedtrace` to also be set.
findings.fix: Change the second line to `GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000,scheddetail=1 ./app  # + per G/M/P` (the runtime docs define scheddetail only in combination with schedtrace=X).

findings.summary: The `findRunnable()` lookup order names the netpoller as a work source two pages before the netpoller is explained.
findings.evidence: Page 5 flow diagram nodes ["runnext","local runq","global runq","netpoller","steal"] and table row ["4","netpoller","epoll check"]; page 7 is where it is first defined: "Network reads and writes park the goroutine, not the thread."
findings.fix: Add a half-line gloss at step 4 on page 5 — "netpoller: goroutines whose network I/O is now ready (page 7)" — so the step is meaningful before the full treatment arrives.

findings.summary: Page 6 ends with a `LockOSThread` code snippet that has no supporting explanation until page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 6 final block is only code: "runtime.LockOSThread() / defer runtime.UnlockOSThread() / // OpenGL ctx, Linux namespaces, UI toolkits"; page 7 supplies the explanation: "`LockOSThread` pins a goroutine to its M. Needed for OS thread-local state only. Always pair with `UnlockOSThread` in a `defer`."
findings.fix: Move the code snippet to page 7 next to those bullets (or move the bullets to page 6), keeping the pin/unpin explanation with the example.

findings.summary: Page 6 defers partial deadlock to a "leak page" that does not exist anywhere in this content.
findings.evidence: Page 6 Q&A: "Partial deadlock is a leak, not a panic — see the leak page." No slide in this part covers leaks; the last page is "Patterns That Hold Up in Production".
findings.fix: Either drop the cross-reference or name the destination explicitly (e.g. "covered in the leaks part of this handbook") so a reader of this part is not hunting for a page that isn't here.

findings.summary: Page 7 ends with the stack-overflow fatal error message before the stack limit and its unrecoverability have been stated.
findings.evidence: Page 7 code: "runtime: goroutine stack exceeds / 1000000000-byte limit / fatal error: stack overflow", with no surrounding text; the limit is introduced on page 8 (table ["64-bit","1 GB"]) with the sidebox "Unrecoverable": "Blowing the limit is fatal, not a panic."
findings.fix: Move the error-message code block to page 8, directly after the "Hard Limits" table and "Unrecoverable" sidebox, so the output illustrates a limit the reader has just seen.

findings.summary: The runtime constant was renamed from `_StackMin` to `stackMin` years ago, so the named identifier is wrong for any current Go source.
findings.fix: Write "`stackMin = 2048` in `runtime/stack.go` — the 2 KB constant (named `_StackMin` before the Go 1.16-era runtime renaming)". Note: this bullet appears on the page titled "What a Goroutine Actually Is" (slide 1).
